title: Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SSNHL)
desc: Unexplained sensorineural hearing loss of at least 30 dB across three consecutive frequencies within 72 hours — a medical urgency.

blocks.content: This is a medical urgency. Recognize it and act on it immediately.
Unexplained sensorineural hearing loss of at least 30 dB across three consecutive frequencies, occurring within 72 hours. Almost always unilateral.

SSNHL is most often idiopathic but causes include viral cochleitis, microvascular event, autoimmune disease, and — in about 1–2% of cases — acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma). Without treatment, roughly one-third of patients recover spontaneously, one-third recover partially, and one-third have permanent loss. The treatment window is approximately 2–4 weeks from onset. After that, steroids are unlikely to change the outcome.

When a patient calls reporting sudden hearing loss in one ear — regardless of how they describe it, whether "my ear went out," "everything sounds muffled," or "I woke up deaf in one ear" — do not schedule them for a routine appointment weeks out. Get the provider on the line before that patient hangs up.
Audiogram — pure tone thresholds, word recognition score, tympanogram to rule out middle ear effusion as the cause, acoustic reflexes

MRI brain with IAC protocol and gadolinium — required in all cases to rule out acoustic neuroma; this is not optional even when hearing recovers fully. Recovery on steroids alone does not rule out a structural lesion — an acoustic neuroma can produce a temporary steroid-responsive pattern
Labs: CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, RPR, ANA, ESR; Lyme titers in endemic areas
Oral prednisone — first-line; high-dose course (72 pills) with taper
Repeat audiogram approximately one week after completing the prednisone course

Intratympanic dexamethasone — used when oral steroids are contraindicated (diabetes, immunocompromised) or as salvage after incomplete recovery; series of 3–4 weekly injections with audiogram after the series
